chapter_theme: The close of the lament: a vision of the Lord's face with its lotus, eyes of compassion and earrings; the passage beyond the thirty-six tattvas into the bare space where the dark mind dies; the ship of love launched on the sea of knowledge; the three questions, who am I, who are you, who is the Supreme, whose answer ends tapas; the Lord who stands for each as each conceives him; the light seen straight at the forehead; and a closing apology, I do not know even myself, with a plea for the company of the good and a last praise of the five-handed god's feet.
structure_note: Eleven couplets, the last short chapter of the work. 226 to 232 are the final askings; 233 is the poet's apology to the ancients, 234 (a unit from the second edition) asks for good company, 235 sums up the three removals (maya, karma, body), and 236 ends with Ganesha, as Sivavakkiyar's work begins. The refrain எக்காலம் holds to the end.

226.reading: The opened-petalled lotus, the two eyes of compassion and the studded earrings: when will they appear to me?
226.nuance: A face, not a doctrine: the lotus may be the face itself or the seat, and the earrings are the Lord's or the guru's; the verse asks for a sight, which the rest of the work seldom does.

227.reading: Leaving behind the five sixes and the six, in the bare open space, when will the mind that stood in pitch darkness die?
227.nuance: ஐயாறும் ஆறும் is thirty and six, the thirty-six tattvas, as tradition counts them. The mind is itself among the tattvas, so it dies when they are left; மை இருள், the kohl-black darkness, is the primal mala in Siddhanta reading.

228.reading: Launching the ship of love on the sea of knowledge that grace shows, when will I sink in the sea of compassion it kindles?
228.nuance: The sea is doubled: knowledge is the sea sailed and compassion the sea drowned in. The ship is love, so love is the means and sinking the end; the poet wants to go under, not to cross.

229.reading: Who am I, who are you, who is the good Supreme himself: when will I realise this and bring tapas to its end?
229.nuance: Three 'who's, the self, the addressed Lord and the Supreme beyond both, which may mirror the Siddhanta three or the Vedanta distinction of the Lord from Brahman. Tapas ends with the answer, so the answer is the whole point of tapas.

230.reading: However each person saw you and in whatever way they thought of you, you stood for each of them in that very way: when will I know this?
230.nuance: The Lord takes the form each conceiver gives him; the verse grounds the diversity of sects in one Lord without ranking them.

231.reading: The bliss that gives light when one looks and looks: when will I see it straight at the forehead and be fixed there?
231.nuance: நெற்றிக்கு நேர் is plainly 'level with the forehead', before the eyes; tradition takes it as the brow centre, the place in the body where the inner light is seen. The repeated looking (உற்றுற்றுப் பார்க்க) is the practice of 225.

232.reading: As the sun hides the shining stars, when will I see your sight, free of any stain?
232.nuance: The stars are not put out but outshone; the Lord's appearing hides all else by its light, and களங்கமற may qualify the sight or the seer.

233.reading: I do not know even myself; all that I have said in this way, when will I lay before the ancients in homage, so that they accept it?
233.nuance: The poet's apology for the whole lament: the one who has asked two hundred times for knowledge admits he does not know himself. முன்னையோர், those who went before, are the earlier siddhas or the learned.

234.reading: As one removes the poisonous snake and takes the good gem, when will I take as companions the good who have ended the quarrel of words?
234.nuance: A unit from the second edition. The gem is the one said to be in the cobra's hood, taken only when the snake is dealt with. சொற்சரவை echoes நச்சரவை and may be a pun, word-snake, as well as word-quarrel; the good are those who have put disputation away.

235.reading: Removing maya, laying waste the deeds to come, making the body separate, when will I see you?
235.nuance: வருவினை is the karma still to come, not the stored or the ripening kind; the three removals (maya, karma, body) answer to the three malas, with the body standing for the primal one.

236.reading: Praising the paired feet of the five-handed one, setting them in my heart, when will I gain firmness?
236.nuance: ஐஞ்சு கரத்தான், the five-handed, is Ganesha (four hands and the trunk). The work ends where Tamil works usually begin, with the elephant-faced god, and with the plainest devotion after so much that passes beyond it.

links.note: Both pass the thirty-six tattvas on the way to the goal: Tirumular's devotees go beyond the six sixes and shatter maya by grace; Pattiragiriyar leaves the five sixes and the six for the bare space where the dark mind dies. Each counts the tattvas with a multiplication, and in both the step beyond them is the last.

194 resolves 'I', 'you' and the other into the one 'you'; 229 asks the three as open questions, who am I, who are you, who is the Supreme, and makes their answer the end of tapas. The question and its answer stand in the same work.

Tirumular's Lord is perceived to the measure that one contemplates him; Pattiragiriyar's Lord stood for each in the very way each saw and thought of him. Both make the form of the Lord depend on the conceiver without making the Lord many.

Agasthiyar sets the hum of Om at the centre of the brows and tells the disciple to see the fullness there; Pattiragiriyar asks to see the light-giving bliss straight at the forehead and be fixed. The link holds on the coded reading of நெற்றிக்கு நேர் as the brow centre.

Both begin from not knowing oneself: Tirumular did not know himself, the knower, until Nandi said 'you are the one who knows'; Pattiragiriyar, having asked for knowledge through the whole lament, confesses he does not know even himself and bows to those who went before. Tirumular's verse ends in the gift, Pattiragiriyar's in the asking.

Two poets' apologies to the learned: Sivavakkiyar opens by asking all who have learned to forgive the errors of one who recites like a madman; Pattiragiriyar closes by laying all he has said before the ancients and asking when they will accept it.

The elephant-faced god frames both works: Sivavakkiyar begins with worship of the black-faced wish-tree so that arts and knowledge rise in thought; Pattiragiriyar ends by praising the five-handed one's feet and setting them in his heart for firmness. In both the Siddhar's plainest devotion goes to Ganesha.

source_issues: Unit 234 (id siddhar:meynjanap-pulambal:0155-201) is from a second edition: unnumbered in the main edition, without the refrain's question mark, interleaved between 233 and 235.
